title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: Levin was standing some distance away. A nobleman beside him, breathing heavily and hoarsely, and another whose thick boots were creaking, kept him from hearing clearly. He could only faintly catch the marshal's soft voice, then the shrill voice of the malicious gentleman, and then Sviazhsky's voice. They were arguing, as far as he could make out, over the interpretation of the act and the exact meaning of the words: "liable to be called up for trial."

The crowd parted to let Sergey Ivanovitch through to the table. Sergey Ivanovitch waited until the malicious gentleman had finished, then said that he thought the best solution would be to refer to the act itself, and asked the secretary to find it. The act said that in case of disagreement, there had to be a ballot.

Sergey Ivanovitch read out the act and began to explain its meaning, but at that point a tall, stout, round-shouldered landowner with dyed whiskers, in a tight uniform that bit into the back of his neck, cut him off. He stepped up to the table and, striking it with his finger ring, shouted at the top of his voice: "A ballot! Put it to the vote! No need for more talking!" Then several voices broke out all at once, and the tall nobleman with the ring, more and more worked up, shouted louder and louder. But you couldn't make out what he was saying.

He was shouting for the very course Sergey Ivanovitch had proposed; but it was obvious that he hated him and his whole party, and this hatred ran through that whole party, and stirred up in opposition the same vindictiveness — though in a more decorous form — on the other side. Shouts went up, and for a moment everything was in confusion, so that the marshal of the province had to call for order.

"A ballot! A ballot! Every nobleman sees it! We shed our blood for our country!… The confidence of the monarch.… No checking the marshal's accounts; he's not a cashier.… But that's not the point.… Votes, please! Disgraceful!…" furious, violent voices shouted on all sides. The looks and faces were even more violent and furious than the words. They expressed the most implacable hatred. Levin had no idea what it was all about, and he marveled at the passion with which they were arguing whether or not the decision about Flerov should be put to a vote. He forgot — as Sergey Ivanovitch explained to him later — this syllogism: that it was necessary for the public good to get rid of the marshal of the province; that to get rid of the marshal a majority of votes was needed; that to get that majority Flerov's right to vote had to be secured; that to secure recognition of Flerov's right to vote, the interpretation of the act had to be settled.

"And one vote may decide the whole question, and one has to be serious and consistent, if one means to be of use in public life," Sergey Ivanovitch concluded. But Levin had forgotten all that, and it pained him to see all these excellent people, for whom he had respect, in such an unpleasant, vicious state of agitation. To escape that painful feeling, he slipped off into the other room where there was no one except the waiters at the refreshment bar. Watching the waiters busy with washing the crockery and setting out the plates and wine-glasses, seeing their calm and cheerful faces, Levin felt an unexpected sense of relief, as if he'd come out of a stuffy room into fresh air. He began to walk up and down, pleased to look at the waiters. He particularly liked the way one gray-whiskered waiter, who openly looked down on the younger ones and was teased by them in return, was teaching them how to fold napkins properly. Levin was about to strike up a conversation with the old waiter when the secretary of the court of wardship — a little old man whose specialty was knowing every nobleman in the province by name and patronymic — drew him away.
"Please come, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," he said. "Your brother's looking for you. They're voting on the legal point."

Levin walked into the room, was handed a white ball, and followed his brother, Sergey Ivanovitch, to the table where Sviazhsky was standing with a significant, ironical expression, holding his beard in his fist and sniffing at it. Sergey Ivanovitch slid his hand into the box, put the ball somewhere, and, making room for Levin, stopped. Levin stepped up, but having completely forgotten what he was supposed to do, and rather flustered, he turned to Sergey Ivanovitch with the question, "Where do I put it?" He asked softly, at a moment when there was conversation going on nearby, hoping his question wouldn't be overheard. But the people speaking paused, and his improper question was heard. Sergey Ivanovitch frowned.
"That's a matter for each man to decide," he said sternly.

Several people smiled. Levin flushed crimson, hurriedly thrust his hand under the cloth, and put the ball on the right, since it was in his right hand. Once he had, he remembered he should have put his left hand in too, and so he stuck it in — too late — and, more flustered than ever, retreated to the back.

"A hundred and twenty-six for admission! Ninety-eight against!" sang out the voice of the secretary, who couldn't pronounce the letter _r_. Then there was laughter; a button and two nuts were found in the box. The nobleman was granted the right to vote, and the new party had won.

But the old party did not consider themselves beaten. Levin heard them asking Snetkov to stand, and he saw a crowd of noblemen surrounding the marshal, who was saying something. Levin moved closer. In reply Snetkov spoke of the trust the noblemen of the province had placed in him, of the affection they had shown — which he didn't deserve, his only merit being his devotion to the nobility, to whom he had given twelve years of service. Several times he repeated, "I have served to the best of my ability, with truth and good faith — I value your kindness and I thank you," and suddenly he broke off, choking on tears, and walked out of the room. Whether those tears came from a sense of the injustice being done him, or from his love for the nobility, or from the strain of his situation, feeling himself surrounded by enemies, his emotion caught the assembly; most were touched, and Levin felt a tenderness for Snetkov.
In the doorway the marshal of the province bumped into Levin.

"Beg pardon, excuse me, please," he said, as if to a stranger; then, recognizing Levin, he smiled shyly. It seemed to Levin he would have liked to say something but couldn't, for emotion. His face and his whole figure in his uniform with its crosses, and the white trousers striped with braid, as he hurried along, reminded Levin of some hunted animal that sees it's done for. This expression in the marshal's face especially moved Levin, because only the day before he had been at his house on his trustee business and had seen him in all his grandeur — a kind-hearted, fatherly man. The big house with its old family furniture; the rather dirty, far-from-stylish but respectful footmen, plainly old house serfs who had stayed loyal to their master; the stout, good-natured wife in a lace cap and Turkish shawl, fussing over her pretty grandchild, her daughter's daughter; the young son, a sixth-form high school boy, coming home from school and greeting his father, kissing his big hand; the genuine, warm words and gestures of the old man — all of it had stirred in Levin the day before an instinctive feeling of respect and sympathy. This old man was a touching, pathetic figure to Levin now, and he longed to say something kind to him.
"So you're sure to be our marshal again," he said.
"That's not likely," said the marshal, looking around with a scared expression. "I'm worn out, I'm old. If there are men younger and worthier than I am, let them serve."
And the marshal disappeared through a side door.
The most solemn moment was at hand. They were going straight on to the election. The leaders of both parties were counting white and black on their fingers.

The argument over Flerov had given the new party not only Flerov's vote, but also extra time, so they could send for three noblemen who had been put out of action by the other party's maneuvers. Two noble gentlemen with a weakness for strong drink had been gotten drunk by Snetkov's partisans, and a third had had his uniform stolen.

Hearing about it, the new party had moved fast, during the dispute over Flerov, to send some of their men in a sledge to dress the stripped gentleman and to bring along one of the drunk ones to the meeting.
"I've brought one — doused him with water," said the landowner who had gone on this errand to Sviazhsky. "He'll do. He's all right."
"Not too drunk? He won't fall down?" said Sviazhsky, shaking his head.
"No, he's first-rate. As long as they don't give him any more here.… I've told the waiter not to serve him a drop, no matter what."
